HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H & P)

History:
• Presenting complaint: 3-day history of persistent watery diarrhoea.  
• Onset/Dynamics: Began suddenly three days ago; frequency every ~10 minutes; neither improving nor worsening.  
• Associated symptoms:
  – Central peri-umbilical abdominal pain, mild-to-moderate, relieved somewhat after bowel movement.  
  – One episode of vomiting this morning after eating fruit; no haematemesis.  
  – Nausea, stomach “gurgling,” mild sweating; no documented fever.  
  – No visible blood in stool.  
  – Limiting oral intake; likely sub-optimal hydration.  
• Triggers/Context: No clear food trigger identified; patient wonders about new asthma inhaler but clinician advised this is unlikely.  
• Baseline/ROS negatives: No chest pain, no new dyspnoea beyond baseline asthma, able to walk and talk, no radiation of abdominal pain.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma.  
• Allergies: NKDA (No known drug allergies).  
• Medications: Inhaler for asthma (brand recently changed; dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Family history: Father died of colorectal cancer ~10 years ago.  
• Social history: Currently staying home from work due to symptoms; smoking/alcohol not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears able to converse normally via video; alert and oriented.  
• Abdomen: Patient-reported mild central tenderness on self-palpation; no report of guarding, rigidity, or rebound.  
• Cardiopulmonary: No chest pain; baseline asthma symptoms only.  
• Skin: No mention of rash or jaundice.  
• Vitals: Not recorded.

Impression:
Acute infectious gastroenteritis (likely viral or food-borne) presenting with watery diarrhoea, mild abdominal cramps, and single vomiting episode.  
DDx (consistent):  
1. Viral gastroenteritis – most probable given sudden onset, self-limited course, absence of blood/fever.  
2. Bacterial food-borne enteritis – possible; monitor for fever or bloody stools.

Management Plan:
• Hydration: Encourage liberal oral fluids (water, electrolyte solutions).  
• Diet: Light diet as tolerated; avoid dairy, caffeine, alcohol until recovery.  
• Medications: No antibiotics advised at this stage; continue regular asthma inhaler.  
• Monitoring/red flags: Seek in-person GP review or emergency care if any of the following occur: fever ≥38 °C, blood in stool or vomit, persistent vomiting preventing fluid intake, severe abdominal pain, signs of dehydration.  
• Activity: Remain at home until symptoms improve to avoid dehydration and transmission.  
• Follow-up: Re-assess in 24–48 h via GP or urgent care if no improvement or worsening.

Patient Summary:
48-year-old man with asthma presents with 3-day watery diarrhoea, mild central abdominal pain, and one episode of vomiting. Findings are most consistent with self-limited acute gastroenteritis. Supportive care and watchful waiting advised; escalate to in-person evaluation if red-flag features develop.

Key Takeaways:
1. Drink plenty of fluids to replace ongoing losses.  
2. Watch for fever, blood in stool, or increased pain and seek immediate care if they occur.  
3. No antibiotics needed now; most gastroenteritis improves within a few days.

Next Steps:
• Patient to monitor symptoms at home and maintain hydration.  
• Arrange GP appointment if no improvement in 1–2 days or sooner if deterioration.  
• Consider stool culture or further GI evaluation if symptoms persist beyond expected course or if red flags emerge.
